::: {.slideref}
ADS-IDAC 5.0.0 (2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.21974488. OpenPRA: Earthperson, Aras, Farag and Diaconeasa, *Proc. ASME IMECE2023* (2023).
:::

::: {.notes}
Where does it go next? Three threads.

First, a new implementation of the tree core, being brought to byte-identical
agreement with the C++ engine on the reference benchmark.

Second, the destination in the title: integration into the open-source OpenPRA
ecosystem, as its dynamic PRA engine. The modern engine and the web workflow
have been developed for it, and the integration is in progress.

Third, tools to read the output at scale: sequence clustering and interactive
visualization, under active development. Parallel traversal solves the compute
half of the combinatorial problem; reading tens of thousands of sequences is
the other half.
:::

## Conclusions {#conclusions data-section="6"}

::: {style="font-size:0.84em;"}
- **Dynamic PRA was held back by its tooling, not its theory**: engines
  welded to one physics code and bounded by serial traversal.
- **Physics is now a service.** Six endpoints couple a new code, a surrogate
  or a digital twin; one contract and one branching logic serve a PWR and a
  space fission reactor.
- **The tree is traversed in parallel.** A metadata-only scheduler and
  peer-to-peer state exchange, with fault tolerance and live monitoring
  included; measured speedups compound to two orders of magnitude over the
  engine as originally fielded.
- **For advanced reactors** this makes passive-system timing, humans and
  automation in the loop, and sequence sampling at the scale of uncertainty
  quantification tractable on infrastructure practitioners already have.
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.84em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
[Next, and underway: integration into the open-source OpenPRA ecosystem,
from a laboratory capability to community infrastructure.]{style="color:#B40000;"}
:::

::: {.notes}
To conclude. Dynamic PRA has been held back by its tooling, not by its theory:
engines welded to one physics code and limited to one sequence at a time. This
work removes both barriers with two moves that rest on one primitive.

Physics is now a service behind an interface of six endpoints, so the models
an advanced reactor needs, including surrogates and digital twins, connect
without merging code. One interface serves a PWR and a space fission reactor.

And the tree is traversed in parallel. ADS-IDAC now runs anywhere and much
faster, and trees of tens of thousands of sequences are generated in under an
hour.

For advanced reactor safety, that turns dynamic PRA from a research method
into a usable capability. The next step is OpenPRA.
:::

### If asked: prepared answers

If a question is not on this list, do not guess: Alp is on the Teams call and
can take it.

- **Is the code available?** The closing slide carries the DOI of the ADS-IDAC
  5.0.0 release on Zenodo. For access and licensing, Alp is the person to
  write to. [thank-you]
- **How is this different from RAVEN, ADAPT, MCDET or EMRALD?** Simulator
  neutrality is not new; ADAPT has it by design. What is different is the form
  of the coupling: a documented service contract with in-memory state exchange
  and typed branching semantics, together with a parallel traversal engine and
  crew cognition in one platform. [Backup: where this sits]
- **Why HTTP and not a linked library?** Isolation. A service shares no
  compiler and no process with the engine, so coupling a new code is
  implementing endpoints, not merging code. The in-process interface is still
  there, and RELAP5 uses it. [solver-interface; Backup: the contract in full]
- **What does the HTTP hop cost?** The paper does not report it. The validated
  RELAP5 path stays in process; an external code pays one request per advance.
  [rest-contract]
- **Have you coupled SAM, or any advanced reactor code?** Not yet. Two
  services speak the contract today, a lumped PWR and a space reactor model,
  and RELAP5 runs in process behind the same five calls. An advanced reactor
  system code needs a wrapper that implements the six endpoints, and the code
  must be able to save and restore its complete state. [rest-contract;
  two-reactors]
- **Does the browser workflow run the IDAC crew?** No. Its branching comes
  from scheduled operator actions and trip firings; the cognitive branching is
  in the C++ engine, which drives the same solvers through the same contract.
  [browser-workflow]
- **Is the space reactor NASA's SR-1?** It is a model built from the public
  description of SR-1 Freedom: HALEU fuel, heat pipes, a closed Brayton
  converter at twenty kilowatts electric, and Hall thrusters. Little of the
  design is public, so every other value is an assumption. It is
  representative, not a design model, and its numbers say nothing about SR-1
  itself. [Backup: the space fission reactor]
- **Is that spacecraft crewed?** No. Onboard fault protection responds first,
  and ground commands arrive after the light time. What matters for dynamic
  PRA is the responder slot: in remote and autonomous operation a software
  policy sits where the control-room crew sits. [two-reactors; Backup: the
  space fission reactor]
- **The paper describes a liquid-metal loop, Stirling conversion and
  seventeen control variables?** That was the model when the paper was
  written. It has since been rebuilt from the public description of SR-1
  Freedom, and the contract did not change. [two-reactors]
- **Are the speedups inflated by the serial optimizations?** No: the slide
  shows each factor as its own step. Parallel speedups are counted against the
  optimized serial run on the same machine and build, and each cluster number
  says what it is counted from. [perf-workstation; Backup: three baselines]
- **Why is the 156 times conservative?** The 752 seconds were timed on a
  modern workstation with a solid-state disk, and about half of that time went
  to re-reading the same files. On slower or shared storage the original
  engine took longer. [perf-workstation]
- **What is the modern toolchain?** GNU Fortran at full optimization. The
  reference Intel build ran RELAP5 without optimization, so this step alone is
  two to two and a half times. [Backup: measured performance]
- **Which machines?** An 8-core Linux workstation and a 14-core Apple-silicon
  laptop. [Backup: three baselines]
- **What exactly is the MPI factor?** 21.4 seconds on one core of the laptop
  against 4.8 seconds on ten ranks: 4.46 times, rounded to about four on the
  slide. [perf-workstation; Backup: laptop wall times]
- **Why does parallelism pay more on realistic scenarios?** A wider and deeper
  tree keeps more workers busy. On the benchmark the tree runs out of branches
  near ten ranks; on the 35,000-sequence tree the engine keeps 94 to 98
  percent of ideal scaling up to 768 ranks. [large-trees-efficiency; Backup: the rank ladder]
- **The paper reports only 1.7 times across eight nodes?** That benchmark tree
  is deliberately narrowed and runs out of width. On a tree wide enough to
  feed every worker, the tree phase keeps 94 to 98 percent of ideal scaling up
  to 768 ranks, counted from each node type's smallest run. [Backup: the
  benchmark tree across cluster nodes; large-trees-efficiency; Backup: the
  rank ladder]
- **Are these large trees in the paper?** No. The paper reports the
  workstation and the first multi-node measurements. The large trees are from
  Alp's dissertation, NC State 2026, Chapter 3, run on NC State's Hazel
  cluster. [large-trees; Backup: the benchmark tree across cluster nodes]
- **What is the 12.5 days?** A projection: the worker time measured on the
  cluster, added up as if one core of the optimized serial engine ran every
  sequence. [large-trees-efficiency]
- **Why two lines in the scaling chart?** Two kinds of nodes on the same
  cluster: 32-core Intel nodes up to 256 ranks, and 192-core AMD nodes from
  256 to 768. Each line is compared with its own ideal. [large-trees-efficiency;
  Backup: the rank ladder]
- **How do you know a resumed study is correct?** Resume is regression tested
  across execution modes and rank counts: each tested permutation has to
  reproduce the reference sequence counts, and the cluster resume reproduced
  the end states of the straight run. [Backup: checkpoint and resume]
- **Is parallel output the same as serial output?** On the validation cases,
  yes: each rank writes in its own directory, the merge reproduces the serial
  layout, and the tests assert that the merged results agree. [memory-fault]
- **Is the crew model a validated HRA method?** No. IDAC is a cognitive model
  of a crew in a closed loop with the plant. It generates behavior and
  branches; it does not certify human error rates. [Backup: the IDAC crew
  model]
- **What about uncertainty quantification?** The tree resolves the aleatory
  uncertainties into branches. Epistemic uncertainty is an outer loop that
  repeats the tree, so its cost is the number of samples times the cost of a
  tree, and parallel traversal divides the second factor. (Optional: the talk
  before this one in the session, on hierarchical uncertainty propagation, is
  the place to point.) [large-trees-efficiency]
- **Fifty-seven minutes for the whole tube-rupture study?** For the tree. The
  engine's total wall time was 1 h 52 min, because it spent about as long
  merging its output as computing the tree. That limit was removed before the
  35,000-sequence runs, which finish tree, merge and extraction in one job.
  [large-trees-efficiency]
- **Is it 35,613 sequences or about 35,000?** The tree's size differs between
  runs, from 34,918 to 35,613 sequences, about two percent, because staggered
  hardware failures make some forks sensitive to timing. 35,613 is the run
  whose histories are shown; the timings come from several runs. The
  tube-rupture tree reproduces exactly. [large-trees; large-trees-efficiency]
:::
